topic: Bayes' Theorem and Independence: Unlocking Predictive Probability

sections.title: Prerequisite Warm-up: The Concept of Conditional Probability
lecture_lines: Conditional probability is probability given a condition.
It shrinks the sample space to the condition.
Example: knowing a card is red changes outcomes.
animations: Create a sample space box colored #FFFFFF.
Fade in event A as a circle #FF0000.
Fade in event B as a circle #0000FF overlapping A.
Highlight the intersection region with color #00FF00.
Label the intersection as P(A and B).

sections.title: Defining Independence
lecture_lines: Independent events don't affect each other's outcomes.
Condition B does not change probability of A.
Example: coin flips and die rolls are independent.
animations: Display definition: P(A|B) = P(A) for independence.
Show event A #FF0000 inside sample space.
Show event B #0000FF appearing with no overlap change.

sections.title: Introduction to Bayes' Theorem
lecture_lines: Bayes' Theorem reverses conditional probability direction.
It calculates cause from observed effects.
We update our belief with new evidence.
The formula uses prior and evidence probabilities.
It turns data into refined knowledge.
animations: Display formula: P(A|B) = P(B|A) * P(A) / P(B).
Color P(A) and P(B) as #00FFFF for contrast.
Flash the full formula to show equality.

sections.title: Practical Application: The 'Smart Fox' Scenario
lecture_lines: The fox scenario illustrates Bayesian updating.
Start with a prior belief about location.
Incorporate rustling sounds as new evidence.
Calculate the updated probability of the zone.
Bayes' helps us reason with uncertain data.
animations: Show Fox location as a point #FF8C00.
Use line to connect fox and observation.

sections.title: Synthesis & Key Takeaway
lecture_lines: Bayes' Theorem creates a feedback loop.
Use both to master predictive probability.
animations: Show key formula in central box #FFFFFF.
Fade out with a summary statement.
